Build a polymer mesh from polygon layers

Source: R/polymer.R
polymer.Rd

Combine one or more polygon layers into a single triangle mesh, where every input edge from every layer is kept as a chain of mesh edges, and record which input features cover each triangle.

Usage

polymer(
  ...,
  rule = c("nonzero", "evenodd", "positive"),
  engine = "cdtr",
  label = c("mesh", "pip")
)

Arguments

...

Polygon layers. Each can be anything the 'wk' package can read (an 'sf' data frame or sfc, a wk::wkb() or wk::wkt() vector, and so on). Data frames keep their non-geometry columns as attributes.

rule

The fill rule: "nonzero" (the default), "evenodd" or "positive".

engine

The triangulation engine. Only "cdtr" is available.

label

How triangles are labelled: "mesh" (the default) propagates winding numbers over the mesh, "pip" tests each triangle's centroid against every ring, as polymer 0.3.0 did. "pip" is kept for comparison and will be removed.

Value

A polymer object, a list with

  • mesh: a wkpool_tri (see wkpool::new_wkpool_tri()) holding the triangles on a shared vertex pool. The vertex table has an origin column: "input" for input vertices and "crossing" for vertices inserted where input edges cross.

  • index: a data frame with one row per triangle and covering feature: triangle (row in mesh), layer (position of the layer in ...) and feature (row within that layer).

  • layers: a list with one data frame of attributes per layer (no geometry).

  • crs: the coordinate reference system shared by the inputs.

Details

All the inputs' edges are triangulated together in one constrained Delaunay triangulation. Where edges from different features cross, the crossing is inserted as a new vertex, so the mesh is a partition of the plane that respects every input boundary. Vertices are shared on exact coordinate equality before triangulation.

Each triangle is then labelled with the features that cover it. The winding number of every feature is propagated across the mesh from the outside: stepping over a mesh edge adds or subtracts one for each input edge lying on it, by its direction. This uses no coordinates, so a sliver triangle cannot be mislabelled, and edges not on the walk are checked for agreement, which detects broken noding (a warning is given). Shells are oriented counter-clockwise and holes clockwise first, the first ring of each polygon being its shell, so holes are subtracted. The fill rule then decides which windings count as covered: "nonzero" (any non-zero winding, so a duplicated part stays covered), "evenodd" (odd winding, so a duplicated part cancels, as in polymer 0.3.0) or "positive". Triangles covered by no feature (gaps enclosed by the inputs) are dropped.

The result is the mesh and its index, not a set of polygons. Use fuse() or layer_n() to get polygons back.

Examples

pool <- polymer(A, B, C)
pool
#> polymer mesh:
#> Layers:    3
#> Features:  6
#> Triangles: 42
#> Vertices:  26 (10 at crossings)
#> Overlaps:  15 triangles covered more than once, at most 3 deep
head(pool$index)
#>   triangle layer feature
#> 1        1     1       3
#> 2        1     2       1
#> 3        2     1       1
#> 4        3     1       1
#> 5        4     1       2
#> 6        5     1       4

## the mesh is a 'wkpool' triangle pool
pool$mesh
#> <wkpool_tri[42 triangles, 26 vertices] CRS=NA>

#>  [4] <triangle: 24,15,2>  <triangle: 10,6,17>  <triangle: 23,18,22>

#> [13] <triangle: 13,16,4>  <triangle: 19,21,13> <triangle: 24,2,11> 
#> [16] <triangle: 7,9,10>   <triangle: 3,14,22>  <triangle: 2,15,5>  
#> [19] <triangle: 3,6,14>   <triangle: 6,15,14>  <triangle: 6,5,15>

#> [25] <triangle: 21,19,23> <triangle: 3,18,17>  <triangle: 16,13,21>
#> [28] <triangle: 18,19,17> <triangle: 20,7,10>  <triangle: 20,12,7>
